records.label: Case 1 (Patient A-III:1)

phenotypes.text: limited extension of knees and elbows

records.segregation: Sanger sequencing confirmed segregation with disease; recessive
quotes: Case 1 was a 6-year-old male, the first child of healthy first cousin parents of Algerian origin (Fig. 1A).

When first referred to the neuropaediatric unit, at 5 months of age, the patient had developmental regression with loss of visual contact, abnormal neurological examination with opisthotonous and axial hypotonia.
At last follow-up, at 6 years of age, the patient was not able to sit unassisted, had spastic tetraparesis with limited extension of knees and elbows, and showed no verbal communication.

records.label: Case 2 (Patient A-III:2)
records.segregation: Sanger sequencing confirmed segregation with disease
quotes: She had a cleft soft palate. The patient was admitted at 2 days of age to neonatal intensive care unit due to episodes with eye revulsion, cyanosis and spasms-like movements. EEG showed a suppression-burst pattern (Fig. 3B and C).

At last follow-up at 26 months of age, she had severe developmental delay with axial hypotonia and absence of head control, segmental hypertonia with limited extension of knees and, no visual contact with abnormal eye movements and no verbal communication.

records.label: Case 3 (Patient B-IV:4)

phenotypes.text: limited range of movement in all joints

records.segregation: Sanger sequencing confirmed segregation with disease
quotes: Prenatally detailed scan revealed a liver containing omphalocele, intestinal atresia and right talipes equinovarus. Delivery was at term by caesarean section, and birthweight was 2.900 kg. Examination at birth showed omphalocele and cleft soft palate.
Seizures were first noted at 2 weeks of age in the form of eye twitches and epileptic spasms.
The patient died at the age of 2 years, from failure to thrive and respiratory infection.

records.label: Case 4 (Patient B-IV:1)
records.segregation: Sanger sequencing confirmed segregation with disease
quotes: Case 4 was a similarly affected brother, who passed away at the age of 4 years due to pulmonary infection and severe growth retardation.
At birth, omphalocele and bilateral talipes equinovarus were observed.
He also had failure to thrive, seizures, arthrogryposis and global developmental delay. Seizures were first noted at 2 weeks of age in the form of eye twitches and epileptic spasms.

records.label: Case 5 (Patient C-III:1)

phenotypes.hpo_label: Bilateral tonic-clonic seizure with generalized onset

records.segregation: Sanger sequencing confirmed segregation with disease
quotes: Case 5 was a 12-year-old female, the first child of an apparently healthy first-cousin Turkish couple (Fig. 1C). She had an onset of eyelid-myoclonia at the age of 2 weeks, and 1 week later also showed myoclonic seizures of the upper limbs.
She has a palatine cleft, a talipes on the left side and a conductive hearing loss. She suffers from recurrent fever episodes without any signs of infection.
In Family C, a homozygous 5-bp deletion, c.812_816delTTAAG, leading to a frameshift p.(Val271Aspfs*9) was identified

records.label: Case 6 (Patient C-III:2)
records.segregation: Sanger sequencing confirmed segregation with disease
quotes: He showed a similar phenotype as his older sister (Patient C-III:1), with refractory epilepsy with myoclonic, tonic and tonic-clonic seizures, from the first day of life. As his sister, he had a palatine cleft.

Seizures deteriorated under ketogenic diet and he died from refractory seizures at the age of 2 years. At that time, he had a profound intellectual disability with tetraparesis with increased muscle tonus.

records.label: Case 7 (Patient D-V:2)

phenotypes.text: profound developmental delay, unable to walk
low set ears, broad nasal bridge, mild hypertelorism, thin upper lip

records.segregation: Sanger sequencing confirmed segregation with disease
quotes: Case 7 was a 10-year-old male, the second child of healthy second-cousin parents from Iran with a family history of epilepsy and development delay (Figs 1D and 2J).
First myoclonic seizures were noted within 1 day after birth and EEG showed dysrhythmia. The seizures evolved into epileptic spasms.
He initially showed reduced muscle tone and developed spasticity and dystonia as well as scoliosis later during the disease course.

records.label: Case 8 (Patient D-V:3)
records.segregation: Sanger sequencing confirmed segregation with disease
quotes: She was noted to suffer from epileptic spasms and myoclonic seizures at 7 days of age. EEG showed burst attenuation initially and scattered sharp waves later during the disease course.
At follow-up at 15 months of age, she was able to roll over onto her sides but was unable to sit unsupported. Head circumference at 15 months of age was 44 cm (1.2 cm <3rd centile).
The cervical notch observed in the brain MRI of the proband of Family D is likely unrelated to the GAD1 variant as no other cases in our cohort displayed a similar finding.

records.label: Case 9 (Patient E-III:2)

phenotypes.text: flexion contractures of elbows and knees
no head control or eye contact

records.segregation: Sanger sequencing confirmed segregation with disease
quotes: He was referred to Istanbul University Cerrahpasa Medical Faculty, Pediatric Genetic Department at 2 months of age due to facial dysmorphism, development delay, cleft palate, Hirschsprung disease, and pes equinovarus deformity (Fig. 2).
Epileptic spasms were observed during physical examination. Retrospectively these were present from 1 month of age, but were not recognized as seizures by parents. EEG revealed hypsarrhythmia.
On eye examination, nystagmus, alternating esotropia, and bilateral pale optics disk were observed. Audiogram was normal at birth, but he failed the hearing test performed at 1 year of age.

records.label: Case 10 (Patient E-III:1)
quotes: Case 10 (Patient E-III:1), the first child of the parents of proband Case 9, was born at 29 weeks of gestation, had cleft palate, short neck, narrow thorax, myoclonic seizures, congenital heart disease (large patent ductus arteriosus, small atrial septum defect moderate pulmonary hypertension), abdominal distension and pes equinovarus deformity similar to the proband, and died at postnatal Day 9 due to sepsis (Fig. 2).

At 7 days of age, the family recognized abnormal fast facial twitches with blinking followed by staring.

At last examination, at 6 years of age, her weight was 17 kg, occipital frontal circumference 50 cm with positional plagiocephaly, inverted nipples, hirsutism and severe scoliosis. No dysmorphic facial features were seen.

records.label: Patient with GAD1 deficiency
quotes: Rational therapy with vigabatrin and a ketogenic diet in a patient with GAD1 deficiency.

notes.statement: von Hardenberg et al. (2020) reported treating a patient with GAD1 deficiency with vigabatrin and a ketogenic diet, which they described as a rational therapy.
quotes: Rational therapy with vigabatrin and a ketogenic diet in a patient with GAD1 deficiency.

notes.statement: Neuray et al. (2020) described a developmental and epileptic encephalopathy in 6 patients with biallelic GAD1 variants. Seizures began at 2 to 6 months of age and were mainly focal motor seizures. Patients also had severe developmental delay and reduced muscle tone. Some patients had variable non-CNS features, including skeletal abnormalities, dysmorphic features, and cleft palate.
quotes: A key clinical feature common to all affected individuals was early onset seizures (from 2 to 6 months), predominantly focal motor seizures with and without impaired awareness

presenting with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, characterized by early-infantile onset epilepsy and hypotonia with additional variable non-CNS manifestations such as skeletal abnormalities, dysmorphic features and cleft palate

notes.statement: Neuray et al. (2020) noted that 3 of the 6 patients achieved seizure freedom, yet all still had severe intellectual disability. The authors suggested that GAD1 defects affect development and cognition independently of seizure control.
quotes: despite seizure control (seizure freedom achieved in three of six individuals), all patients described here still showed severe intellectual disability.
We therefore hypothesize that GAD1 mutations may also play an important role in intellectual development.

notes.statement: In 6 patients from 6 unrelated families with developmental and epileptic encephalopathy, Neuray et al. (2020) used exome sequencing to identify biallelic GAD1 variants. Five families carried homozygous variants and 1 family carried compound heterozygous variants. Sanger sequencing confirmed segregation consistent with recessive inheritance.
quotes: The segregation of the variants with the clinical phenotype was confirmed by Sanger sequencing, which showed a recessive mode of inheritance.
Homozygous variants were identified in five families (Families A, B, D, E and F), whereas compound heterozygous variants were found in Family C (Table 2).

notes.statement: Neuray et al. (2020) noted that 4 of the variants affected the PLP-binding domain and that 4 variants were null alleles. In silico analysis predicted reduced protein stability for 2 of the missense variants and disrupted PLP binding for another. Together, these findings supported a loss-of-function mechanism.
quotes: The likely negative impact of the missense variants on PLP-binding and C-terminal catalytic domains, together with the finding of four null pathogenic variants in our case series, supports the idea that the clinical phenotypes observed are likely due to a loss-of-function mechanism.

Further in silico analysis predicted a reduction in protein stability for p.(Phe324Cys) and p.(Asn564Ser), in association with a break in H-bonds in the pyridoxal 5′-phosphate (PLP) binding domain for p.(Thr347Met).

notes.statement: Neuray et al. (2020) noted that, according to gnomAD, GAD1 is moderately intolerant to missense variants (Z-score 2.32) and to predicted loss-of-function variants (9 observed vs 33.1 expected).
quotes: According to gnomAD, GAD1 shows a moderate intolerance to missense variants (Z-score = 2.32; observed 217 and expected 336.5) and predicted loss-of-function variants (expected 33.1, observed 9).

notes.statement: Neuray et al. (2020) questioned whether the homozygous GAD1 S12C variant previously reported in spastic cerebral palsy (Lynex et al., 2004) is pathogenic. They pointed out that pathogenicity predictions for it conflict and that other candidate genes in the linked 2q24-q31.1 region were never investigated. They proposed that GAD1 pathogenic variants cause a distinctive neurodevelopmental disorder rather than spastic cerebral palsy.
quotes: However, the predictions on its pathogenicity are conflicting as it is predicted benign by MutationAssessor, DEOGEN2, and MetaLR.
we emphasize that GAD1 pathogenic variants should be considered the cause of a distinctive neurodevelopmental disorder instead of spastic cerebral palsy (Lynex et al., 2004).

notes.statement: Chatron et al. (2020) found that the c.1414-1G>C GAD1 variant in Family A abolished normal splicing: cDNA analysis showed no normal mRNA product and three aberrant isoforms, with skipping of exon 15, retention of 76 bases of intron 14, or deletion of the first 7 bases of exon 15.
quotes: cDNA analysis confirmed the absence of normal mRNA product with three aberrant isoforms: one with exon 15 skipped, one with 76 bases of intron 14 retained and one with the first seven bases of exon 15 deleted.

notes.statement: Chatron et al. (2020) found that the in-frame p.Lys232del GAD67 variant was expressed at a level comparable to wildtype in a cell-free expression system. They noted that this did not exclude a splicing effect predicted in silico, and considered the variant pathogenic because the family reproduced the knockout mouse phenotype of cleft palate and omphalocele, although loss of function was not formally demonstrated.
quotes: Western blotting of wild-type and p.Lys232del-GAD67, however, revealed that p.Lys232del-GAD67 was expressed at a comparable level as wild-type-GAD67, which is not in favour of an effect on splicing (Supplementary Fig. 3).

The recapitulation of the knockout mouse model phenotype (co-occurrence of cleft palate and omphalocele) in this family, together with phenotypic similarities with the remaining families, is strongly supportive of pathogenicity of this variant, while loss of function could not be formally demonstrated.

notes.statement: Chatron et al. (2020) used structural modeling to predict that the E509K missense variant, which affects a highly conserved residue in the pyridoxal-dependent decarboxylase domain, would disrupt salt bridges with arg316, lys318, and lys389 and no longer fit into the domain core.
quotes: The wild-type glutamate residue is predicted to form salt bridges with the arginine at position 316, the lysine at position 318 and the lysine at position 389.
the mutated amino acid is predicted to no longer fit into the domain core.

notes.statement: Chatron et al. (2020) found that 4 of the 6 families carried homozygous truncating variants, which they considered supportive of a complete loss-of-function mechanism. The GAD1 pRec score of 0.934 in gnomAD was consistent with autosomal recessive inheritance of loss-of-function variants.
quotes: Four of six families carried a homozygous variant leading to a truncated protein (Supplementary Fig. 5), supportive of a complete loss-of-function mechanism.
is 0.934, above the 0.9 threshold to consider a gene intolerant to bi-allelic variants.

notes.statement: Chatron et al. (2020) found the same GAD1 R531X variant in an Iranian family and a Turkish family, and suggested that the variant may lie on a common haplotype given the relative geographic proximity of the two families.
quotes: Families D and E, of Persian and Turkish origin, respectively, shared the same GAD1 c.1591C>T variant leading to a premature stop codon p.(Arg531*)
Given the relative geographical proximity, a common haplotype is possible.

notes.statement: Chatron et al. (2020) observed phenotypic variability between 2 families carrying the identical R531X variant: pes equinovarus, joint contractures, and clefting were absent in Family D. They suggested that genetic background or environmental factors modulating movement in utero might explain this.
quotes: Despite identical mutation in Families D and E, there was some phenotypic variability between both families; in particular there was an absence of pes equinovarus, joint contractures and cleft lip in Family D. This might be influenced by variability in genetic backgrounds or environmental factors that modulate movement in utero.

notes.statement: Chatron et al. (2020) proposed that the cleft palate, omphalocele, pes equinovarus, and joint contractures in GAD1-related disease result from reduced fetal movements. They suggested that these non-neural features are probably secondary to severe CNS involvement, as in Gad1-null mice.
quotes: Also the pes equinovarus, joint contractures and arthrogryposis, seen in several of the patients in our study, are known to reflect a reduction of foetal movements (Hall, 1997). As such, the non-neural phenotypes seen in our cohort of patients should probably be seen as secondary to the severe CNS involvement.

notes.statement: Chatron et al. (2020) observed a good seizure response to vigabatrin in 5 of 7 treated patients. They cautioned that this response may reflect seizure semiology, since patients with epileptic spasms seemed to benefit most, and called for validation of vigabatrin as a targeted treatment and for early genomic sequencing in early-onset seizures.
quotes: Finally, a remarkably good response of seizures to vigabatrin was seen in five of seven individuals who were treated with the drug.
It should be noted however, that this good response seems to be driven by seizure semiology, as particularly patients with epileptic spasms appeared to benefit from vigabatrin.

notes.statement: Chatron et al. (2020) reported that seizures began in the first 2 months of life in all 11 patients, mainly as epileptic spasms or myoclonic seizures. Seven of 8 patients with neonatal EEGs showed suppression-burst or burst attenuation, and the 2 patients first recorded later showed hypsarrhythmia. Increased muscle tone was described as a core feature, often together with axial hypotonia.
quotes: EEG at onset showed suppression-burst or variant with interburst attenuation pattern (Case 8, Patient D-V:3) in seven of eight patients who had recordings during the neonatal period, and hypsarrhythmia in two patients who only had a first EEG taken later in disease course.
A remarkably increased muscle tone was a core clinical feature seen in all patients.

notes.statement: Asada et al. (1997) generated Gad67-null mice. The mice were born at the expected frequency but died of severe cleft palate during the first morning after birth. In the cerebral cortex of the newborn mutant mice, GAD activity was reduced to 20% and GABA content to 7% of normal, but the brain showed no discernible defects.
quotes: These mice were born at the expected frequency but died of severe cleft palate during the first morning after birth.
GAD activities and GABA contents were reduced to 20% and 7%, respectively, in the cerebral cortex of the newborn GAD67 -/- mice. Their brain, however, did not show any discernible defects.

notes.statement: Asada et al. (1997) stated that their findings were the first demonstration of a role for GAD67-derived GABA in the development of nonneural tissue. They noted that, by contrast, their Gad65-null mice had normal brain GABA content and normal behavior, apart from a slight increase in susceptibility to seizures.
quotes: this is the first demonstration of a role for GAD67-derived GABA in the development of nonneural tissue
Recently we have produced GAD65 -/- mice and demonstrated that lack of GAD65 does not change brain GABA contents or animal behavior, except for a slight increase in susceptibility to seizures.
